title: The Online Shop You Built Yourself

start.title: Orders for 1 Baht
start.bestWhy: Briefly closing the store to contain the situation first, then finding the root cause from evidence, will cost fewer customers than guessing your way through fixes or rewriting everything from scratch.
start.text: This morning you open the admin panel of your self-built online store and find 38 orders totaling just 1 baht — despite products priced in the hundreds to thousands. All of them came from a handful of new accounts within 20 minutes, while regular customers are still shopping normally. What do you do first?
start.source: NIST SP 800-61 (Incident Response Guide: containment → root cause elimination → recovery)

choices.label: Temporarily close the store and investigate what happened before doing anything else.
choices.out: You close the storefront for about 6 hours. Some customers are frustrated they can't order, but the attacker can't place more orders either — and you now have time to read the logs without them being overwritten.
u: Store closed for 6 hours — some customers don't wait.
choices.lesson: Contain first (containment): stop the damage from spreading, then find the root cause. A short, purposeful closure is better than patching blindly when you don't yet know what's wrong.

choices.label: Cancel all the 1-baht orders and keep the store open.
choices.out: The day looks quiet and customers notice nothing — but you still can't answer how the prices were manipulated in the first place.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Deleting the results is not the same as fixing the root cause. If the vulnerability that was exploited is still there, the attacker will just do it again.

choices.label: Change the admin password and force all accounts to reset their passwords — you suspect a credential leak.
choices.out: Customers forced to reset their passwords find it annoying, and the logs you read later show that no one's credentials were stolen at all.
u: Forced password reset — some customers drop off.
choices.lesson: Base your hypothesis on evidence, not gut feeling. The attacker didn't guess passwords — they exploited a loose rule. Fixing the wrong thing wastes time and erodes trust.

choices.label: Close the store and rewrite the entire system from scratch to make it secure.
choices.out: You close the store for two weeks to rewrite everything. Many existing users move to competitors while waiting, but you're confident the new system won't have the same flaw.
u: Store closed for two weeks — existing customers move to competitors.
choices.lesson: A full rewrite looks safe but is costly and risky — code written in a rush tends to introduce new vulnerabilities. Finding the root cause and patching precisely is usually the smarter path.

investigate.title: Finding the Root Cause
investigate.bestWhy: There are two root causes happening simultaneously — both must be closed, otherwise the remaining one can still be exploited.
investigate.text: From the logs (system activity records) you find that the attacker never guessed anyone's password. Using developer tools built into every browser (DevTools), they sent order-creation commands directly to the database and inserted their own prices. There are two simultaneous root causes: (1) the database permission rules (Rules) allow any logged-in user to edit any field of any order, and (2) the total price is calculated in the customer's browser (client-side) and the backend server (Server) trusts that value without verifying it. How do you fix this?
investigate.source: OWASP Top 10: Broken Access Control, Insecure Design

choices.label: Tighten the Rules so only necessary fields can be written, and move price calculation and payment handling to the Server — then reopen the store.
choices.out: You spend one day tightening the Rules so users can only submit item lists and quantities, while the Server reads prices from the product database and calculates totals itself. You then try to manipulate the price several ways — none of them work anymore.
u: Store closed for another half day.
choices.lesson: Key principle: never trust data from the client side. Anything involving money or permissions must be decided at the Server, and Rules should allow only the minimum necessary access (least privilege).

choices.label: Fix the Rules first to be strict — deal with server-side price calculation later.
choices.out: The new Rules block direct writes to the database. You reopen the store ahead of schedule, but the checkout flow still trusts prices sent by the browser.
u: Brief store closure.
choices.lesson: A half-fix creates a false sense of security — the second vulnerability is still open. You need to close every root cause you've found.

choices.label: Move price calculation to the Server first — leave the Rules alone for now because you're worried about breaking something.
choices.out: Prices are now calculated server-side, so the 1-baht orders disappear. You reopen the store without touching the Rules that are still wide open.
u: Brief store closure.
choices.lesson: Fear of breaking something shouldn't be a reason to leave a vulnerability open. Test the fix on a copy first, then apply it — don't just leave it.

partialClient.title: The Second Hole Gets Exploited
partialClient.bestWhy: Price calculation must genuinely move to the Server. Browser-side checks can always be bypassed by an attacker.
partialClient.text: Five days later, the new Rules block direct database writes — but the attacker adapts. They modify the price value in the payment request sent by the webpage, which the system still trusts. They acquire 12 items at a fraction of the real cost. The store loses money and stock runs out.

u: Items purchased at manipulated prices — stock depleted, real customers can't buy.

partialClient.source: OWASP Top 10: Insecure Design (never trust data from the client side)

choices.label: Move price calculation to the Server immediately — the Server reads prices from the product database only and does not accept prices from the client.
choices.out: You close the second hole completely. You try to manipulate the price several ways and the system rejects all of them.
u: Store closed to apply the fix.
choices.lesson: Data coming from the client is a "request," not a "fact." The Server must calculate and verify everything on its own, every time.

choices.label: Add browser-side code to check that the submitted price matches what's displayed on the page.
choices.out: The check looks fine in normal use, but the attacker isn't using your interface — they send requests directly to the API, bypassing the check within the hour.
u: Attacker bypasses the client-side check successfully.
choices.lesson: Client-side validation improves the user experience, but it is not security — attackers have full control over their own client.

partialRules.title: Customer Data Leaked
partialRules.bestWhy: Close the hole completely right away, check what data leaked, and notify customers so they can protect themselves.
partialRules.text: Five days later, prices are calculated server-side — but the Rules still let any logged-in user read everyone else's data. The attacker sends commands directly to the database and pulls the names, addresses, and phone numbers of 2,100 customers. A group of customers then starts receiving spam.

u: Customers receiving spam — some stop using the store.

choices.label: Close the hole immediately, fix the Rules completely, check the logs to see what data was accessed, then notify all affected customers.
choices.out: You fix the Rules and email all 2,100 customers explaining what leaked and what to watch out for. Some are angry, but many thank you for being upfront.
u: Some customers leave after being notified.
choices.lesson: Notifying affected users honestly hurts in the short term, but it lets them protect themselves and builds long-term trust. (International data protection law such as the EU's GDPR requires notifying the supervisory authority within 72 hours and notifying affected individuals when the risk is high.)

choices.label: Fix the Rules quietly and don't announce anything — there's no evidence the data has been misused yet.
choices.out: The store returns to normal and there's no news at first — but customers who received spam have no idea their data leaked, so they can't protect themselves.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Staying silent doesn't make the problem go away — it just hides the damage until it surfaces, and when it does, the trust loss will be far worse.

choices.label: Close the store and bring in an external expert to audit the entire system before making any announcement.
choices.out: The expert finds two additional weaknesses and helps confirm exactly what data was leaked. You announce with a clear remediation plan, but the store has to stay closed for a long time at significant cost.
u: Extended closure — some customers don't wait.
choices.lesson: External experts are worth it when you're unsure of the damage scope — but you need to weigh the cost against the time your store has to stay closed.

repeat.title: Attacked Again
repeat.bestWhy: Being attacked again means the root cause was never fixed. Stop, fix everything properly, and communicate honestly.
repeat.text: A few days later, abnormal-price orders are back — and this time some customers report receiving strange messages that know their name and address. The original vulnerability is still open, and data may have leaked. What do you do?

choices.label: Temporarily close the store, fix both root causes completely (Rules + server-side pricing), then communicate openly about what happened.
choices.out: You close the store, fix both the Rules and the server-side pricing completely, then make an honest announcement about what happened. Customers are upset, but most see that you're taking responsibility.
u: Store closed — some customers lost from the news.
choices.lesson: Being attacked again means the first round didn't fix the root cause. Stop, review the evidence, fix everything completely, and communicate straightforwardly.

choices.label: Fix the technical issues completely, but don't tell anyone — you don't want to alarm customers.
choices.out: The system is genuinely more secure now and the store looks quiet — but customers whose data leaked have no idea and aren't protecting themselves.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Concealing an incident doesn't protect customers — it only delays the day the truth comes out.

choices.label: Run a discount campaign and give out coupons to win customers back — fix the system later.
choices.out: Orders spike immediately, but the attacker can see the vulnerability is still open and starts exploiting it every day right alongside real customers.
u: Coupons bring some customers back.
choices.lesson: Polishing your image without fixing the system just delays the problem — and it comes back harder.

rewrite.title: New Store, New Holes
rewrite.tag: New Vulnerabilities from a Rushed Build
rewrite.bestWhy: Close the admin panel vulnerabilities before going live — multiple layers (login rate limiting + a second factor) are safer than waiting for something to go wrong.
rewrite.text: Two weeks later the new store launches. Prices are now calculated server-side and the Rules are far tighter. Some customers come back on the news of the launch — but in the rush, you forgot to change the admin panel's default password and didn't limit failed login attempts. A bot (automated program) is now trying to guess the admin password about 3,000 times per hour.

u: Some customers return following the relaunch news.

rewrite.source: CISA Secure by Design (no default passwords); NIST SP 800-63B (limit login attempts)

choices.label: Change the default password, enable two-factor authentication (2-step) for the admin account, and limit failed login attempts.
choices.out: The bot keeps trying but gets blocked after just a few failed attempts — and even if it guesses the password right, it still can't get in without the code from your phone.
u: Customers feel confident as the store stays stable.
choices.lesson: Defence in depth: rate limiting + a second factor means a weak or leaked password is no longer a single point of failure.

choices.label: Only change the default password to a longer one.
choices.out: A longer password helps a lot, but the bot can still try an unlimited number of times — and there's still no second factor if the password is phished.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: A strong password is a good first layer — but it shouldn't be the only layer.

choices.label: Don't do it right now — need to push the store promotion first, and no one has broken in yet.
choices.out: First-day orders are excellent — but that night the bot successfully guesses the admin password.
u: Promotional campaign pays off.
choices.lesson: A risk that hasn't materialized yet is not a risk that doesn't exist. A bot actively guessing passwords is clear evidence the store is already being targeted.

wave2.title: Phishing Email
wave2.bestWhy: Check through a channel you navigate yourself — not a link in the email — and add a second factor to important accounts.
wave2.text: About a week passes. The previously exploited vulnerabilities are closed, but the attacker changes tactics. You receive an email claiming to be from your hosting provider, saying your account will be suspended in 24 hours if you don't click a verification link. The logo and wording look completely genuine.
wave2.source: CISA Secure Our World (phishing and 2-step); Verizon DBIR

choices.label: Don't click the link. Open the provider's website by typing the address yourself, check whether there's a real alert on your account, and enable 2-step for all admin accounts.
choices.out: There are no alerts on the real account. You recognize it as phishing, enable 2-step for all admin accounts, and warn the team not to click links in emails like this.
u: Store stays stable — customers return.
choices.lesson: An urgent email + a link is the classic phishing signal. Always verify through a channel you navigate yourself. 2-step protects you even if your password is stolen.

choices.label: Click the link — if it looks real, enter your password, because you're afraid of the account being suspended.
choices.out: The page is a fake that captures your password. A few hours later someone logs into your hosting account and your store's admin panel using those credentials.
u: No visible effect yet.
choices.lesson: Urgency is a phishing tool. Reusing the same password in multiple places means one compromise takes down everything.

choices.label: Delete the email and do nothing more.
choices.out: You dodge this one — but you haven't checked your accounts or added a second factor. If a more convincing email comes next, there's nothing to fall back on.
u: No additional incidents.
choices.lesson: Not being fooled this time doesn't mean you're safe. Adding a second factor (2-step) means a leaked password won't bring down the whole system.

takeover.title: Admin Account Hijacked
takeover.bestWhy: You need to cut the attacker off from every access point — sessions, tokens, everything — not just change the password. Then audit what they changed.
takeover.text: The attacker is inside the admin panel using a legitimate admin account. They modified product prices, changed the payment receiving account to their own, and viewed customer data — all without exploiting a single line of code.

u: Prices and payment account altered — many customers lost.

takeover.source: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet; NIST SP 800-61

choices.label: Revoke all sessions, change passwords on all accounts, enable 2-step, audit the logs to see what was changed, revert every altered value, and notify customers.
choices.out: You go through every change one by one, restore the original payment account, close every access point, and customers receive a direct notification.
u: Store closed for remediation — some customers leave after being notified.
choices.lesson: When an account is hijacked, you must cut the attacker off from every access point — active sessions, tokens, and keys — not just change the password. Then audit everything they touched.

choices.label: Change the password only, then reopen the store.
choices.out: The attacker still holds an active session that hasn't expired. They come back the next night and change the payment account again.
u: Brief closure to change the password.
Attacker returns via the still-active session.
choices.lesson: Changing the password alone isn't enough. If the attacker still has an active session (a login that's still alive), they can keep coming in. You must log them out of every device.

choices.label: Hire an external security team to audit the entire backend, then follow their recommendations.
choices.out: The team discovers the attacker planted a hidden admin account. They remove it, set up 2-step, and customers are notified. Costly, but thorough.
u: Extended closure and audit fees — some customers don't wait.
choices.lesson: Attackers often leave a "backdoor" behind. Expert eyes can find things you'd miss on your own — but it comes at a cost in time and money.

news.title: The Story Breaks
news.bestWhy: If you missed the disclosure window, admit it and act as soon as you realize. The longer you stay silent, the more expensive trust becomes to rebuild.
news.text: A customer posts that they've been receiving spam that mentions their name and the address they used to shop at your store. The post is shared thousands of times overnight and people start asking whether the store knew about this.

u: News breaks that the store covered up the incident.

news.source: EU GDPR Article 34 (notification of affected individuals)

choices.label: Issue a public statement acknowledging what happened, what data leaked, what has been fixed, and advise customers to watch out for spam and change their passwords.
choices.out: You admit you knew earlier and didn't notify anyone. The criticism is heavy — but the clear information keeps some customers on your side.
u: Some customers leave after learning they were kept in the dark.
choices.lesson: If you missed the disclosure, fix it the moment you realize. Late transparency is still better than none.

choices.label: Deny any connection to your store.
choices.out: Users cross-reference the data and find it matches your store. The denial gets shared as a textbook example of irresponsible handling.
u: Caught denying verifiable facts.
choices.lesson: Denying verifiable facts turns a data incident into a full-blown credibility crisis.

choices.label: Close the store for three days to investigate before issuing any statement.
choices.out: You confirm the full scope of the damage before speaking — but during those three silent days, the rumours travel further than the facts.
u: Three days of silence — rumours spread.
choices.lesson: Verifying before speaking is good — but if you go silent too long, rumours will tell the story for you.

wave2_blocked.title: Phishing That Failed
wave2_blocked.text: The following week, a phishing email impersonating your hosting provider reaches your team. One admin already entered their password on the fake page — but the attacker can't get into the account, because every admin account has 2-step enabled. You receive an alert about a login attempt from an unknown device.

u: Customers see the store running smoothly — no incidents.

wave2_blocked.source: Microsoft Security: MFA blocks nearly all automated account takeovers

choices.label: View summary
choices.out: You change that admin's password and remind the team to stay alert. No damage is done.
u: No damage.
choices.lesson: A second factor means one person's mistake doesn't become a disaster for the whole store.

root.title: A Trustworthy Store Builder
root.desc: You fixed the root causes, layered your defences, and the store still has nearly as many users as before. Customers see a store that handled an incident systematically.

rebuilder.title: The Architect Who Started Over
rebuilder.desc: You took the most expensive path — a full rewrite — and still caught the new vulnerabilities that came with the rush. The store is secure, but the user base is not the same.

honest.title: Honest but Bruised
honest.desc: The store took a serious hit, but you told customers the truth. The trust that remains is the foundation for a comeback.

survivor.title: A Survivor Who Learned
survivor.desc: The store is still running and the critical holes are closed — even if there were costs along the way.

nomfa.title: Strong on Fixes, Forgot the Second Layer
nomfa.desc: The code vulnerabilities are patched, but the admin account still relies on a password alone. The remaining risk is a human one, not a code one.

cover.title: Covered It Up and Lost the Trust
cover.desc: The system may have been fixed — but not telling customers only delayed the damage, and when it hit, it hit harder.

scarred.title: Deep Wounds, Still Standing
scarred.desc: The store's data and assets took serious damage. It's still alive, but rebuilding customer trust will take a long time.

bleeding.title: Bleeding Out
bleeding.desc: You chose to attract customers with promotions instead of fixing the system. The attacker exploits the same hole every day. The store is slowly collapsing with no end to the incident in sight.

collapse.title: The Store Had to Shut Down
collapse.desc: The user count dropped too low for the store to survive. Look back and see which decision caused the biggest drop.

AXES.dL: You tend to keep the store open first, even when risk remains.
AXES.dR: You're willing to sacrifice short-term revenue to secure the system first.
AXES.dM: You strike a reasonable balance between security and keeping the store open.

AXES.dL: You prefer to verify before acting. The upside is precision; the downside is speed.
AXES.dR: You decide quickly. The upside is stopping incidents fast; the downside is missing things.
AXES.dM: You adjust your pace well to the demands of each situation.

AXES.dL: You tend to prioritize image — which often erodes trust later.
AXES.dR: You tell users the truth, even when it stings in the short term.
AXES.dM: You haven't faced many situations that forced a clear communication choice yet.

AXES.dL: You tend to choose the fast fix, which sometimes leaves the root cause untouched.
AXES.dR: You think about root causes and long-term consequences.
AXES.dM: You mix quick patches with root-cause fixes.
